title: D-Day: From Midnight Gliders to the Beaches of Normandy
alt_titles: D-Day Hour by Hour: How the Normandy Landings Unfolded
The D-Day Gamble: Weather, Deception and Five Beaches
D-Day: The 24 Hours That Opened the Western Front
thumbnail_file: Into the Jaws of Death 23-0455M edit.jpg
description_summary: Just after midnight on 6 June 1944, British gliders landed beside a canal bridge in Normandy. By nightfall, about 156,000 Allied troops were ashore. This is the story of D-Day: the plan, the deception, the weather gamble, and what happened on Utah, Omaha, Gold, Juno and Sword.

scenes.narration: At sixteen minutes past midnight on Tuesday the sixth of June 1944, a wooden glider crash-landed beside a canal bridge in Normandy. Inside were British soldiers led by Major John Howard. Howard's glider landed with a heavy jolt, yards from its target. More gliders landed close behind. Within about ten minutes, the bridge and a second one nearby were in British hands.

It was the first action of D-Day. Over the next few hours, thousands of paratroopers dropped behind the coast. Nearly seven thousand ships and landing craft crossed the English Channel. Thousands of Allied aircraft flew overhead. From dawn, about one hundred and fifty six thousand Allied troops would come ashore on five beaches.

shots.caption: The five D-Day beaches and the airborne landing zones

scenes.narration: This is the story of D-Day: the plan, the gamble on the weather, and the long hours on the beaches. It was the largest seaborne invasion in history. And it came close to being postponed for weeks. Its outcome would decide whether the Allies could return to western Europe.

Troops crossing to the beaches of Normandy, June 1944

scenes.narration: By 1944, Nazi Germany had occupied France for four years. Britain, the United States and Canada planned to open a new front in western Europe. The operation was code-named Overlord. Its supreme commander was the American general Dwight D. Eisenhower. More than two million Allied personnel took part in the wider operation.

shots.caption: General Dwight D. Eisenhower, 1944
Allied assault routes across the Channel, US Army map

scenes.narration: Germany expected an invasion. Hitler had ordered a chain of coastal defences called the Atlantic Wall. The strongest fortifications guarded the major ports. Field Marshal Erwin Rommel strengthened the defences in Normandy. He added mines and beach obstacles, and stakes in open fields to wreck any gliders that tried to land.

shots.caption: German beach obstacles in Normandy, May 1944
Beach obstacles in Normandy, June 1944

scenes.narration: The shortest crossing was to the Pas-de-Calais, and the Germans expected the attack there. The Allies chose Normandy instead. To keep the Germans guessing, a deception plan called Fortitude invented a whole army in south-east England, supposedly led by General George Patton. Fake radio traffic even suggested a separate attack on Norway.

shots.caption: A dummy tank of the kind used to fool German reconnaissance

scenes.narration: Normandy had no big port the Allies could capture quickly, so they planned to bring their own. Huge concrete sections would be towed across the Channel and sunk off the coast. They would form artificial harbours, known as Mulberries. One was planned for the American beaches, and one for the British at Arromanches.

shots.file: File:The Mulberry artificial harbour at Arromanches in Normandy, June 1944. A24675.jpg
shots.caption: The Mulberry harbour under construction, June 1944

card.text: Ports built in Britain and towed to France

shots.file: File:The Mulberry artificial harbour off Arromanches in Normandy, September 1944. BU1024.jpg
shots.caption: The Mulberry harbour off Arromanches, September 1944

scenes.narration: The invasion needed the right tides and enough light. Eisenhower picked the fifth of June. But on the fourth, high winds, rough seas and low cloud made landings impossible. With ships already loaded, Eisenhower postponed the invasion by a day. His commanders gathered at Southwick House, near Portsmouth, to decide what to do next.

stick.label: 4 June: a storm in the Channel

shots.caption: Storm conditions in the Channel

scenes.narration: Eisenhower's chief weather forecaster was an RAF officer, Group Captain James Stagg. The forecasting teams had not always agreed. Stagg predicted a short break in the storm on the sixth. Weather stations in the west of Ireland helped spot it coming. If they waited, the next suitable tides were around two weeks away. Eisenhower decided to go.

shots.caption: Group Captain James Stagg

scenes.narration: German forecasters saw the same storm. The Luftwaffe's chief meteorologist expected rough seas to last until mid-June. Many senior German officers left their posts for exercises. Rommel drove home to Germany, partly for his wife's birthday. He took her a pair of shoes from Paris. He was not in Normandy when the invasion began.

shots.caption: Field Marshal Erwin Rommel

scenes.narration: On the fifth of June, Eisenhower wrote a short note in case the landings failed. It said the troops had done all that bravery could do. It ended with one line. If any blame or fault attaches to the attempt, it is mine alone.

stick.label: 5 June: a note, just in case

shots.query: Eisenhower in case of failure note
shots.caption: Eisenhower's 'in case of failure' note, US National Archives

card.text: If any blame or fault attaches to the attempt it is mine alone.

scenes.narration: That evening, Eisenhower visited American paratroopers of the 101st Airborne Division as they prepared to leave England. A photograph of him talking with them became one of the best-known images of the war. Hours later, they were in the air.

shots.caption: Eisenhower talks with paratroopers, 5 June 1944

shots.file: File:Eisenhower talks with 502 PIR in England.jpg
shots.caption: Eisenhower with men of the 502nd Parachute Infantry, England

shots.file: File:US Paratrooper of 101st Airborne Division climbing aboard a C-47.jpg
shots.caption: A 101st Airborne paratrooper boards a C-47

scenes.narration: After midnight, more than thirteen thousand American paratroopers jumped over the Cotentin peninsula, behind Utah Beach. Cloud and anti-aircraft fire scattered many of them miles from their targets. Small groups gathered in the dark and fought for whatever objectives they could reach.

shots.file: File:C-47s fly low over Utah Beach c6 June 1944.jpg
shots.caption: C-47 transport planes over Utah Beach, June 1944

scenes.narration: On the eastern flank, the British 6th Airborne Division landed around the river Orne. Howard's men held the two bridges until paratroopers reinforced them. Others attacked the gun battery at Merville, which had to be silenced before the invasion ships came close.

shots.caption: Gliders beside the canal bridge, June 1944
The canal bridge, soon renamed Pegasus Bridge, June 1944
The Merville battery

scenes.narration: At first light, Allied warships and bombers pounded the coast, aiming to knock out the German guns before the troops arrived. Then, at half past six, American troops began landing on the two western beaches, Utah and Omaha. The British and Canadian beaches, Gold, Juno and Sword, followed about an hour later.

shots.caption: Supplies and troops on a Normandy beach, June 1944

scenes.narration: At Utah, the landing craft came ashore too far south of their planned spot. It turned out to be lucky. The defences there were weaker. The 4th Infantry Division's casualties that day were around two hundred, the lightest of any beach.

shots.caption: American troops land on Utah Beach
Landings on Utah Beach, 6 June 1944

scenes.narration: Omaha was different. The beach lay beneath steep bluffs, with German positions overlooking the sand. In the low cloud, much of the air bombing had fallen too far inland. Many defences were untouched when the first troops arrived.

shots.caption: A landing craft heads for Omaha Beach, 6 June 1944
The bluffs above Omaha Beach

shots.file: File:Smoking LCVP off Omaha Beach 6 June 1944.jpg
shots.caption: A landing craft off Omaha Beach, 6 June 1944

scenes.narration: At Omaha, things went wrong from the start. Thirty two amphibious tanks were launched about four and a half kilometres out. Twenty seven sank in the rough sea, and thirty three crewmen were lost. Landing craft were swept off course. Many men had to wade ashore under heavy fire, weighed down by their equipment.

card.label: Amphibious tanks that sank off Omaha

shots.caption: Troops wading ashore at Omaha

scenes.narration: Nineteen men from the small town of Bedford, Virginia, were among the first to land. For hours, the attack seemed stuck at the water's edge. Then small groups of soldiers began working their way up the bluffs. By nightfall, the Americans held a narrow foothold. About two thousand of them had been killed or wounded on Omaha that day.

shots.caption: Omaha Beach later on D-Day
Landing ships unloading on a Normandy beach, June 1944

scenes.narration: West of Omaha, about two hundred US Rangers under Lieutenant Colonel James Rudder climbed thirty metre cliffs at Pointe du Hoc. The big guns they had come to destroy had been moved. They found them in an orchard inland and put them out of action.

shots.caption: US Rangers at Pointe du Hoc, June 1944
Lieutenant Colonel James Rudder
The cliffs at Pointe du Hoc

scenes.narration: On Gold Beach, the British 50th Division landed at about twenty five past seven. Within days, one of the Mulberry harbours would rise just off this stretch of coast, at Arromanches. The division suffered about a thousand casualties on D-Day.

shots.caption: Men of the British 50th Division, Normandy 1944

shots.query: British forces invasion of Normandy 6 June 1944
shots.caption: British troops during the invasion, 6 June 1944

scenes.narration: At Juno, the 3rd Canadian Division faced rough seas and strong defences. It suffered nearly a thousand casualties. But by nightfall, Canadian troops had pushed further inland than any other Allied force. Some came within sight of Carpiquet airfield, near Caen.

shots.caption: Canadian troops land on Juno Beach

shots.file: File:Follow-up waves of the 9th Canadian Infantry Brigade disembarking with bicycles from landing craft onto 'Nan White' sector of Juno Beach at Bernieres-sur-Mer, 6 June 1944. A23938.jpg
shots.query: 9th Canadian Infantry Brigade Juno Beach bicycles
shots.caption: Canadian troops with bicycles come ashore at Juno, 6 June 1944

scenes.narration: On Sword, the easternmost beach, British troops landed from half past seven. Commandos marched inland to relieve Howard's men at the bridges. Germany's nearest tank division only received its orders at about nine in the morning. Hitler had kept tight control of his armoured reserves.

shots.file: File:Landing on Queen Red Beach, Sword Area.jpg
shots.caption: British troops on Sword Beach, 6 June 1944

shots.file: File:Royal Marine Commandos attached to 3rd Division for the assault on Sword Beach move through Colleville-sur-Orne on their way to relieve forces at Pegasus Bridge, Normandy, 6 June 1944. B5067.jpg
shots.caption: Commandos head inland to relieve the men at Pegasus Bridge

card.text: German tanks finally get their orders

scenes.narration: By the end of the day, about one hundred and fifty six thousand Allied troops had landed in Normandy by sea and air. The Atlantic Wall had been broken in a single day. But the price had been high, and the battle was far from over.

shots.file: File:Troops come ashore on one of the Normandy invasion beaches, past the White Ensign of a naval beach party, 7 June 1944. A24012.jpg
shots.caption: Reinforcements come ashore, 7 June 1944

card.label: Troops ashore by the end of 6 June
card.note: US, British, Canadian and other Allied forces

scenes.narration: Around ten thousand Allied soldiers were killed, wounded or missing on D-Day. Research by the National D-Day Memorial Foundation has identified 4,414 who died, including 2,501 Americans. German losses are estimated at between four and nine thousand.

shots.file: File:Unknown soldier grave in Normandy American Cemetery and Memorial.jpg
shots.caption: A grave of an unknown soldier, Normandy

scenes.narration: Not every goal was met. The city of Caen, meant to fall on the first day, held out for weeks. Only Gold and Juno had joined up by nightfall. All five beachheads were not linked until the twelfth of June.

shots.file: File:Newsmap Monday June 12, 1944 - map showing the Normandy landings.jpg
shots.caption: A US Army 'Newsmap' of the landings, 12 June 1944

scenes.narration: Over the following weeks, the Allies poured men, vehicles and supplies through the Mulberry harbour and across the beaches. The Battle of Normandy lasted into August. Paris was liberated on the twenty fifth of August 1944. The battle cost tens of thousands of lives on all sides, including about twenty thousand French civilians.

shots.caption: Crowds celebrate the liberation of Paris, August 1944

scenes.narration: Eisenhower's note was never needed. It was saved, and it survives today in the US National Archives. The misdated line at the top, July instead of June, is a small sign of the pressure he was under.

shots.caption: Eisenhower in Normandy, June 1944

scenes.narration: Today, war cemeteries line the Normandy coast, for soldiers of every army that fought there. The American cemetery stands on the bluffs above Omaha Beach, the stretch of sand that came closest to failing. Every year on the sixth of June, families and visitors gather along the coast to remember them.

shots.caption: The Normandy American Cemetery above Omaha Beach
The Commonwealth war cemetery at Bayeux
Omaha Beach today

scenes.narration: D-Day did not end the war. Fighting in Europe went on for almost another eleven months. But it opened a western front at last, and began the liberation of western Europe. It all started with a few gliders, landing in the dark. Sources and image credits are in the description.

shots.caption: The Pegasus Bridge memorial today
